title: GLOMAP
summary: Global Structure-from-Motion: camera poses and a sparse point cloud

blocks.text:
Notebook 02 gave pairwise matches. Here they become one consistent scene: a pose (position and orientation) for every frame, refined camera intrinsics, and a sparse point cloud with one 3D point per feature track. The poses tell the Gaussian Splatting trainer where each frame was taken from, and the sparse points are where the Gaussians start.

The result goes to `work/sparse/0/` in COLMAP's binary format, plus `work/sparse_points.ply` for viewing in other programs.

import shutil, time
from collections import Counter
from pathlib import Path

import cv2
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import plotly.graph_objects as go
import pycolmap

pycolmap.logging.minloglevel = 2      # errors only (logs go to the Jupyter terminal)

PROJECT_DIR = Path.cwd()
WORK_DIR = PROJECT_DIR / "work"
IMAGES_DIR = WORK_DIR / "images"                      # input  (notebook 01)
DATABASE_PATH = WORK_DIR / "database.db"              # input  (notebook 02), never modified here
GLOBAL_DB_PATH = WORK_DIR / "database_global.db"      # working copy that calibration modifies
SPARSE_DIR = WORK_DIR / "sparse"                      # output: sparse/0, sparse/1, ...

image_names = sorted(p.name for p in IMAGES_DIR.iterdir() if p.suffix.lower() in {".jpg", ".jpeg", ".png"})
N = len(image_names)
position = {name: i for i, name in enumerate(image_names)}   # name -> index in time order
print(f"{N} images, database: {DATABASE_PATH.stat().st_size / 1024**2:.0f} MB")
194 images, database: 218 MB

## Incremental vs. global SfM

The classic COLMAP mapper is incremental. It reconstructs two images with many matches, then adds one image at a time: solve for the new camera from 3D points it already sees (PnP), triangulate new points, run bundle adjustment, repeat. It's robust but slow, because bundle adjustment runs again and again on a growing problem, and small errors can drift along the sequence.

GLOMAP, now part of COLMAP as the global mapper, solves for all cameras at once:

| Step | What happens |
|---|---|
| **View graph calibration** | Estimate the focal length from the fundamental matrices of many pairs. (No EXIF here, so COLMAP only has a guess.) |
| **Relative poses** | For each pair, compute the *essential matrix* E, which gives the relative **rotation** and the **direction** of movement. It does *not* give the distance: one pair of images can't tell a small object nearby from a large one far away. |
| **Rotation averaging** | Find one rotation per camera that agrees best with *all* pairwise rotations at once. Pairs that disagree by more than 10° are thrown out as outliers. |
| **Track establishment** | Chain matches across images into **tracks**: "this keypoint in images 3, 4, 5, 9 and 12 is the same physical point". |
| **Global positioning** | GLOMAP's key idea: solve camera **positions** and 3D **points** *together*, using only the viewing directions from cameras to points. This also fixes the unknown distances. |
| **Bundle adjustment (BA)** | The final polish. Adjust all poses, all points and the intrinsics so that every 3D point, projected into every image that sees it, lands as close as possible to the detected keypoint. That distance is the **reprojection error**. |
| **Retriangulation** | Recover more points with the refined cameras, then adjust again. |

Since everything is solved together, outliers and weakly connected images are its weak spot: a bad link has nowhere to hide. If the view graph falls apart, GLOMAP returns several separate models. I wanted to see how it handles the low part at the end, where the band in notebook 02 narrows.

## Estimating the focal length

`calibrate_view_graph` changes the database in place: it overwrites the intrinsics and re-labels the pair geometries. So I run it on a copy and leave the database from notebook 02 untouched. That way this notebook can be re-run with other settings without matching again.

for suffix in ("", "-wal", "-shm"):
    Path(str(GLOBAL_DB_PATH) + suffix).unlink(missing_ok=True)
shutil.copy2(DATABASE_PATH, GLOBAL_DB_PATH)

Config = pycolmap.TwoViewGeometryConfiguration

def describe_database(path):
    with pycolmap.Database.open(path) as db:
        camera = db.read_all_cameras()[0]
        _, geometries = db.read_two_view_geometries()
    return camera, Counter(Config(g.config).name for g in geometries)

camera_before, configs_before = describe_database(GLOBAL_DB_PATH)
print("camera before:", camera_before)
print("pair configurations before:", dict(configs_before))

camera before: Camera(camera_id=1, model=OPENCV, width=1920, height=1080, params=[2304, 2304, 960, 540, 0, 0, 0, 0] (fx, fy, cx, cy, k1, k2, p1, p2))
pair configurations before: {'UNCALIBRATED': 1845, 'PLANAR_OR_PANORAMIC': 163}

The calibration re-estimates each pair's relative pose with the new focal length and keeps it only if there are enough inliers: at least 30, making up at least 25 % of the matches.

With the full video these defaults cut the chain. The weak links in the low-angle part (24–50 inliers) were labelled `DEGENERATE`, and GLOMAP returned 6 separate models. Lowering the thresholds to 15 inliers and 10 % kept everything in one model, but the trained model was still poor in that section, so in the end I cut it from the video (notebook 01). On the first 580 frames the defaults give one model, so I use them as they are.

`random_seed` makes RANSAC repeatable.

calibration_options = pycolmap.ViewGraphCalibrationOptions()   # defaults: ≥ 30 inliers, ≥ 25 % of the matches
calibration_options.random_seed = 0

t0 = time.time()
ok = pycolmap.calibrate_view_graph(GLOBAL_DB_PATH, calibration_options)
print(f"calibration {'succeeded' if ok else 'FAILED'} in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s")

camera_after, configs_after = describe_database(GLOBAL_DB_PATH)
print("camera after :", camera_after)
print("pair configurations after:", dict(configs_after))

focal length guess    :    2304 px  → horizontal field of view 45°
focal length estimate :    1762 px  → horizontal field of view 57°

The calibration moved the focal length well below the 2304 px guess, but it's still above the ~1550 px expected from the lens (notebook 02). Bundle adjustment refines it further below.

The pair labels changed too:

- `CALIBRATED`: a reliable relative pose with the new focal length. These pairs drive GLOMAP.
- `DEGENERATE`: no reliable relative pose (too few inliers, or almost no camera movement). These are ignored.
- `UNCALIBRATED` and `PLANAR_OR_PANORAMIC` stay as they were. They still help build tracks.

## Running GLOMAP

`global_mapping` runs all the steps above and writes each model it finds to `work/sparse/<n>/`. Since COLMAP 4.2 every connected component of the view graph becomes its own model, so a split shows up directly. Old results are deleted first.

if SPARSE_DIR.exists():
    shutil.rmtree(SPARSE_DIR)
SPARSE_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)

mapping_options = pycolmap.GlobalPipelineOptions()
mapping_options.random_seed = 0

t0 = time.time()
reconstructions = pycolmap.global_mapping(
    database_path=GLOBAL_DB_PATH,
    image_path=IMAGES_DIR,
    output_path=SPARSE_DIR,
    options=mapping_options,
)
print(f"GLOMAP done in {time.time() - t0:.0f} s, {len(reconstructions)} model(s)\n")

for model_id, rec in sorted(reconstructions.items()):
    idx = sorted(position[im.name] for im in rec.images.values())
    print(f"model {model_id}: {rec.num_reg_images():3d} images (time index {idx[0]}–{idx[-1]}), "
          f"{rec.num_points3D():6,d} points, mean reprojection error {rec.compute_mean_reprojection_error():.2f} px")

GLOMAP done in 91 s, 1 model(s)

model 0: 194 images (time index 0–193), 52,425 points, mean reprojection error 0.91 px
Using model 0: 194 of 194 images registered (100 %)

## What came out

### Camera intrinsics

Bundle adjustment refined the focal length again and estimated the lens distortion. I also compare the focal length with the value from the lens, 18 mm on the 600D's 22.3 mm wide sensor:

cam = rec.cameras[next(iter(rec.cameras))]
fx, fy, cx, cy, k1, k2, p1, p2 = cam.params
print(cam)
print(f"\nfocal length : fx = {fx:.0f} px, fy = {fy:.0f} px → horizontal FOV {horizontal_fov(cam):.1f}°")
print(f"distortion   : k1 = {k1:+.3f}, k2 = {k2:+.3f} (radial), p1 = {p1:+.4f}, p2 = {p2:+.4f} (tangential)")

SENSOR_WIDTH_MM, LENS_MM = 22.3, 18          # Canon EOS 600D, kit lens at 18 mm
lens_fx = LENS_MM / SENSOR_WIDTH_MM * cam.width
print(f"from the lens: fx = {lens_fx:.0f} px → estimate is {(fx / lens_fx - 1) * 100:+.1f} % off")

- The estimate lands within about 1 % of the lens value, from the images alone.
- `fx ≈ fy`, so the pixels are square, as they should be.
- `k1 < 0` is barrel distortion: straight lines bow outwards towards the edges, which the kit lens does at 18 mm. Notebook 04 removes it.
- `cx, cy` stay at the image centre, because GLOMAP doesn't refine the principal point by default.

Where a regular grid ends up through the estimated lens:

grid_u, grid_v = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(0, cam.width, 17), np.linspace(0, cam.height, 10))
ideal = np.stack([grid_u.ravel(), grid_v.ravel()], axis=1)
# Undistorted pinhole pixel -> normalized ray -> distorted pixel (using the camera model)
rays = np.stack([(ideal[:, 0] - cx) / fx, (ideal[:, 1] - cy) / fy], axis=1)
distorted = cam.img_from_cam(np.hstack([rays, np.ones((len(rays), 1))]))

plt.figure(figsize=(10, 6))
plt.scatter(*ideal.T, s=8, c="gray", label="ideal pinhole grid")
plt.scatter(*distorted.T, s=8, c="red", label="where the lens actually puts it")
for a, b in zip(ideal, distorted):
    plt.plot([a[0], b[0]], [a[1], b[1]], c="red", lw=0.6)
plt.gca().invert_yaxis(); plt.axis("equal"); plt.legend(loc="upper right")
plt.title("Estimated lens distortion")
plt.show()

### The 3D scene

Points carry the image colours. Cameras are small pyramids coloured by time, from dark blue at the start of the video to yellow at the end. Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom.

def camera_frustums(rec, scale, names):
    # Line segments for a small pyramid per camera, in world coordinates.
    xs, ys, zs, colors = [], [], [], []
    for name in names:
        im = rec.find_image_with_name(name)
        cam = rec.cameras[im.camera_id]
        world_from_cam = im.cam_from_world().inverse()
        w, h = cam.width, cam.height
        corners_px = np.array([[0, 0], [w, 0], [w, h], [0, h]], dtype=float)
        corners_cam = np.hstack([(corners_px - [cam.principal_point_x, cam.principal_point_y])
                                 / [cam.focal_length_x, cam.focal_length_y], np.ones((4, 1))]) * scale
        apex = world_from_cam * np.zeros(3)
        corners = np.array([world_from_cam * c for c in corners_cam])
        for a, b in [(apex, corners[0]), (apex, corners[1]), (apex, corners[2]), (apex, corners[3]),
                     (corners[0], corners[1]), (corners[1], corners[2]), (corners[2], corners[3]), (corners[3], corners[0])]:
            xs += [a[0], b[0], None]; ys += [a[1], b[1], None]; zs += [a[2], b[2], None]
            colors += [position[name]] * 3
    return xs, ys, zs, colors

def plot_reconstruction(rec, max_points=40_000, title=""):
    pts = np.array([p.xyz for p in rec.points3D.values()])
    rgb = np.array([p.color for p in rec.points3D.values()])
    if len(pts) > max_points:
        keep = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(pts), max_points, replace=False)
        pts, rgb = pts[keep], rgb[keep]
    names = sorted((im.name for im in rec.images.values()), key=position.get)
    centers = np.array([rec.find_image_with_name(n).projection_center() for n in names])
    scale = 0.03 * np.linalg.norm(np.percentile(centers, 95, axis=0) - np.percentile(centers, 5, axis=0))
    fx_, fy_, fz_, fc = camera_frustums(rec, scale, names)
    fig = go.Figure([
        go.Scatter3d(x=pts[:, 0], y=pts[:, 1], z=pts[:, 2], mode="markers",
                     marker=dict(size=1.2, color=[f"rgb({r},{g},{b})" for r, g, b in rgb]), name="points"),
        go.Scatter3d(x=fx_, y=fy_, z=fz_, mode="lines",
                     line=dict(color=fc, colorscale="Plasma", width=2), name="cameras"),
    ])
    fig.update_layout(title=title, height=700, margin=dict(l=0, r=0, t=40, b=0),
                      scene=dict(aspectmode="data", xaxis_visible=False, yaxis_visible=False, zaxis_visible=False))
    fig.show()

plot_reconstruction(rec, title=f"GLOMAP: {rec.num_reg_images()} cameras, {rec.num_points3D():,} points")

What I checked here: the pumpkin sits inside the ring of cameras, the camera path is smooth with no camera jumping away from the rest, and the table is flat rather than bent (bending would point to wrong distortion or drift). The orientation is arbitrary, since SfM doesn't know where up is. Notebook 07 deals with that.

## Quality checks

### Reprojection error

For each observation of a 3D point in an image, the reprojection error is the pixel distance between where the point projects and where the keypoint was detected. Bundle adjustment minimises exactly this. One frame, with green dots at the detected keypoints and red lines towards the projections, magnified 20×:

def show_reprojection(name, magnify=20, max_points=600):
    im = rec.find_image_with_name(name)
    cam = rec.cameras[im.camera_id]
    observed, projected = [], []
    for p2d in im.points2D:
        if p2d.has_point3D():
            xyz = rec.points3D[p2d.point3D_id].xyz
            observed.append(p2d.xy)
            projected.append(cam.img_from_cam(im.cam_from_world() * xyz))
    observed, projected = np.array(observed), np.array(projected)
    err = np.linalg.norm(projected - observed, axis=1)

    img = cv2.cvtColor(cv2.imread(str(IMAGES_DIR / name)), cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)
    plt.figure(figsize=(14, 8)); plt.imshow(img); plt.axis("off")
    pick = np.random.default_rng(0).choice(len(observed), min(max_points, len(observed)), replace=False)
    for o, p in zip(observed[pick], projected[pick]):
        plt.plot([o[0], o[0] + magnify * (p[0] - o[0])], [o[1], o[1] + magnify * (p[1] - o[1])], c="red", lw=0.8)
    plt.scatter(*observed[pick].T, s=4, c="lime")
    plt.title(f"{name}: {len(observed)} observations, median error {np.median(err):.2f} px "
              f"(red lines ×{magnify})")
    plt.show()

show_reprojection(image_names[N // 4])

point_errors = np.array([p.error for p in rec.points3D.values()])
track_lengths = np.array([p.track.length() for p in rec.points3D.values()])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(15, 4))
axes[0].hist(point_errors, bins=np.linspace(0, 4, 81), color="tab:blue")
axes[0].axvline(np.mean(point_errors), c="red", ls="--", label=f"mean {np.mean(point_errors):.2f} px")
axes[0].set_xlabel("mean reprojection error per 3D point (px)"); axes[0].legend()
axes[1].hist(track_lengths, bins=np.arange(2, 40), color="tab:green")
axes[1].axvline(np.mean(track_lengths), c="red", ls="--", label=f"mean {np.mean(track_lengths):.1f} images")
axes[1].set_xlabel("track length (number of images seeing the point)"); axes[1].legend()
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Most points are well under 1 px. Track length is the number of images that see a point; GLOMAP requires at least 3.

### Points per image

Images that observe few 3D points are only loosely tied into the reconstruction:

obs_per_image = np.array([rec.find_image_with_name(n).num_points3D if n in registered else 0 for n in image_names])

plt.figure(figsize=(15, 3))
plt.bar(range(N), obs_per_image, width=1.0, color=np.where(obs_per_image < 100, "red", "tab:blue"))
plt.axhline(100, c="red", ls=":", label="100 (weak)")
plt.xlabel("image (time order)"); plt.ylabel("3D points observed"); plt.legend()
plt.title("Observed 3D points per image (0 = not registered)")
plt.show()

weakest = int(np.argmin(np.where(obs_per_image > 0, obs_per_image, np.inf)))
print(f"weakest registered image: {image_names[weakest]} with {obs_per_image[weakest]} points")
show_reprojection(image_names[weakest])
weakest registered image: frame_00512.jpg with 88 points

## Comparison with incremental COLMAP

Setting `RUN_INCREMENTAL = True` runs the classic incremental mapper on the same matches (the database from notebook 02) and writes to `work/sparse_incremental/`. The later notebooks always use the GLOMAP result. With the full video, the incremental mapper took about twice as long as GLOMAP and split into 3 models at the low-angle section.

RUN_INCREMENTAL = False

if RUN_INCREMENTAL:
    INC_DIR = WORK_DIR / "sparse_incremental"
    INC_DB_PATH = WORK_DIR / "database_incremental.db"
    shutil.rmtree(INC_DIR, ignore_errors=True); INC_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)
    shutil.copy2(DATABASE_PATH, INC_DB_PATH)         # the mapper writes intrinsics back, so use a copy

    t0 = time.time()
    inc = pycolmap.incremental_mapping(INC_DB_PATH, IMAGES_DIR, INC_DIR)
    t_inc = time.time() - t0
    inc_id, inc_rec = max(inc.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1].num_reg_images())
    print(f"incremental: {t_inc:.0f} s, {len(inc)} model(s); largest has {inc_rec.num_reg_images()} images, "
          f"{inc_rec.num_points3D():,} points, error {inc_rec.compute_mean_reprojection_error():.2f} px")
    print(f"GLOMAP     : {rec.num_reg_images()} images, {rec.num_points3D():,} points, "
          f"error {rec.compute_mean_reprojection_error():.2f} px")
    print("incremental intrinsics:", inc_rec.cameras[next(iter(inc_rec.cameras))])
    plot_reconstruction(inc_rec, title="Incremental COLMAP")
else:
    print("Skipped (set RUN_INCREMENTAL = True to run it).")
Skipped (set RUN_INCREMENTAL = True to run it).

## Saving

GLOMAP already wrote the model in COLMAP's binary format. Notebook 04 reads `work/sparse/0`, so if the largest model has another index it's copied there. The points also go to `work/sparse_points.ply`, which opens in Blender, MeshLab or CloudCompare.

MODEL_DIR = SPARSE_DIR / "0"
if model_id != 0:
    # Make the chosen (largest) model the one at sparse/0
    shutil.rmtree(MODEL_DIR, ignore_errors=True)
    MODEL_DIR.mkdir(parents=True)
    rec.write(MODEL_DIR)

check = pycolmap.Reconstruction(MODEL_DIR)
print(f"{MODEL_DIR.relative_to(PROJECT_DIR)}: {sorted(p.name for p in MODEL_DIR.iterdir())}")
print(f"  {check.num_reg_images()} images, {check.num_points3D():,} points")

rec.export_PLY(WORK_DIR / "sparse_points.ply")
print(f"exported {(WORK_DIR / 'sparse_points.ply').relative_to(PROJECT_DIR)}")

## Result

One model with all 194 frames, about 52,000 points and a mean reprojection error of about 0.9 px. The focal length came out about 1 % above the 1550 px from the lens, and the distortion is the barrel shape expected at 18 mm. With the full video the default calibration thresholds split the scene; without the low-angle section they work as they are.
